phy_edx.10.0.summary: When two different insulating materials are rubbed together, **friction transfers electrons** from one material to the other; protons never move because they are fixed in the nucleus. The material that **gains electrons becomes negatively charged** and the material that **loses electrons is left with an equal positive charge**, so the total charge stays the same. Charged objects exert non-contact forces on each other: **like charges repel and unlike charges attract**, and the force is stronger when the charges are bigger and closer together. This topic is triple (separate) physics only.

core.p: All materials are made of atoms. An atom has a tiny nucleus containing **protons (positive charge)** and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by **electrons (negative charge)**. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel.
bullets: Relative charge: proton +1, electron -1, neutron 0.
Protons are held in the nucleus and **cannot be removed by rubbing**.
Electrons are on the outside of the atom, so outer electrons can be **transferred** from one material to another.
An uncharged (neutral) object still contains huge numbers of charges; it just has **equal amounts** of positive and negative charge.
An object becomes charged only when it has **more or fewer electrons than protons**.

callouts.p: In static electricity, charging always happens by the transfer of electrons. Positive charge never moves.

core.h: Why insulators can be charged by friction
core.p: In an **electrical insulator**, electrons are not free to move through the material. When electrons are transferred onto or off the surface by rubbing, they **stay where they are**, so the charge builds up on the surface. This build up of charge that does not flow is called **static electricity**.
bullets: Examples of insulators used in experiments: **polythene**, **acetate**, Perspex, rubber balloons, wool, nylon.
In a conductor such as a metal, electrons are free to move, so any charge spreads out and can flow away (for example through your hand), so it is hard to charge a conductor you are holding.
The word static means not moving: the charge stays on the insulator.
Only the parts of an insulator that were rubbed become charged.

callouts.p: Electric charge that builds up on the surface of an insulator and does not flow.

core.p: When two **different** insulating materials are rubbed together, the friction between them brings their surfaces into close contact and **electrons are transferred** from the atoms of one material to the atoms of the other. Which way the electrons move depends on the two materials.
bullets: Rubbing does work against friction, which provides the energy to move electrons between surfaces.
One material **gains electrons**, the other **loses electrons**.
The number of electrons gained by one equals the number lost by the other.
No charge is created or destroyed: charge is only **transferred**.
The same rod rubbed with a different material may gain or lose electrons depending on the pairing.

callouts.p: When two insulators are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one material to the other, so both become charged.

core.p: The material that **gains electrons** now has more electrons than protons, so it becomes **negatively charged**. The material that **loses electrons** now has more protons than electrons, so it is left with an **equal positive charge**.
bullets: Gains electrons, so excess of negative charge, so **negative**.
Loses electrons, so fewer electrons than protons, so **positive**.
The two charges are **equal in size and opposite in sign**.
The positive object has not gained protons or positive charge; it has **lost electrons**.
If 2 electrons move from the cloth to the rod, the rod has a charge of -2 units and the cloth +2 units.

callouts.p: Never write that positive charges moved onto the rod. An object becomes positive by losing electrons.

core.h: Example 1: polythene rod rubbed with a cloth
core.p: When a **polythene rod** is rubbed with a cloth (such as a wool duster), **electrons are transferred from the cloth to the polythene**. The polythene rod gains electrons and becomes **negatively charged**; the cloth loses electrons and is left **positively charged**.
bullets: Electrons move: cloth to polythene.
Polythene: gains electrons, so negative.
Cloth: loses electrons, so equal positive charge.
A rubber balloon rubbed on hair behaves the same way: the balloon gains electrons (negative) and the hair loses electrons (positive).

callouts.p: Polythene: think 'P for pulls in electrons', so it goes negative. Acetate does the opposite.

core.h: Example 2: acetate rod rubbed with a cloth
core.p: When an **acetate rod** is rubbed with a cloth, **electrons are transferred from the acetate to the cloth**. The acetate loses electrons and becomes **positively charged**; the cloth gains electrons and becomes **negatively charged**.
bullets: Electrons move: acetate to cloth (the opposite direction to polythene).
Acetate: loses electrons, so positive.
Cloth: gains electrons, so equal negative charge.
This shows that the direction of electron transfer depends on the **pair of materials**, not on which one is the rod.

core.p: Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only moved. So when two neutral objects are rubbed together, the total charge before (zero) equals the total charge after (zero): one object is negative and the other has an **equal positive** charge.
bullets: Total charge before = 0; total charge after = (+Q) + (-Q) = 0.
The size of the charge on each object depends on **how many electrons** were transferred.
Rubbing harder or for longer can transfer more electrons, giving a bigger charge on each object.
This is why the rod and cloth always end up with **opposite** charges, so they attract each other.

callouts.p: The material losing electrons is left with a positive charge equal in size to the negative charge on the material gaining electrons.

core.p: Charged objects exert **electrostatic forces** on each other without touching: this is a **non-contact force**. The direction of the force depends on the types of charge.
bullets: **Like charges repel**: positive and positive, or negative and negative, push apart.
**Unlike charges attract**: positive and negative pull together.
The forces act on **both** objects, equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton's third law).
The force is **larger when the objects are closer together**.
The force is **larger when the charges are bigger**.
A charged rod and the cloth it was rubbed with attract each other because they have opposite charges.

callouts.p: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

core.h: Demonstrating the forces with suspended rods
core.p: A classic class demonstration shows both rules. One charged rod is hung from a thread so it can turn freely; a second charged rod is brought close to one end without touching.
bullets: Rub a polythene rod with a cloth and hang it in a paper stirrup from a thread so it can rotate.
Bring a second rubbed polythene rod near one end: the hanging rod **turns away** (both negative, so they **repel**).
Bring a rubbed acetate rod near it instead: the hanging rod **turns towards** it (positive and negative, so they **attract**).
The rods do not touch, showing the force is **non-contact**.
The closer the rods, the faster and further the hanging rod turns, showing the force increases as the distance decreases.
Hanging the rod reduces friction so even a small electrostatic force can make it move.
Use dry conditions: damp air allows charge to leak away.

core.p: You can find the charge on an unknown object by seeing whether it is attracted or repelled by an object of known charge.
bullets: If it is **repelled** by a negative polythene rod, it must be **negative**.
If it is **repelled** by a positive acetate rod, it must be **positive**.
**Repulsion is the only sure test** for charge type, because attraction could also happen with a neutral object (studied later in static phenomena).
Always state which rule you used: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions, start from the transfer of electrons, then state the resulting charges, then apply the force rule.

core.h: Linking it all together for 6 mark answers
core.p: Top answers give a clear chain of reasoning from particles to forces.
bullets: Both materials start neutral: equal numbers of protons and electrons.
Rubbing causes friction, which transfers electrons from one insulator to the other.
The material gaining electrons becomes negative; the one losing electrons is left with an equal positive charge.
Charge stays on the surface because the materials are insulators.
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract; the force is non-contact and is bigger when closer.
So the rod and cloth attract each other, and two identically charged rods repel.

callouts.p: Do not say protons or positive charges move, and do not say charge is made by rubbing.

analogy.p: Imagine two children each holding the same number of red marbles (protons, glued down in their pockets) and blue marbles (electrons, loose in their hands). When they wrestle (rub), some blue marbles are pulled from one child to the other. The child who grabbed extra blue marbles now has more blue than red (negative); the other child has more red than blue (positive), by exactly the same number, because no marbles were created or lost. Where it breaks down: in reality the charges also push and pull each other from a distance (like charges repel, unlike attract), which marbles do not do, and which material grabs electrons depends on the materials, not on which is stronger.

terms.d: Negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; the only particle transferred when insulators are charged by friction.
Positively charged particle in the nucleus; it does not move during charging by friction.
Having equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so no overall charge.
Material in which electrons are not free to move, so charge stays where it is placed.
Material in which electrons are free to move, so charge can flow through it.
Charge that builds up on an insulator and does not flow.
Rubbing two different insulators together so electrons transfer from one to the other.
Having gained electrons, so more electrons than protons.
Having lost electrons, so fewer electrons than protons.
Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred; rubbed objects get equal and opposite charges.
Non-contact force between charged objects.
Push apart; happens between like charges.
Pull together; happens between unlike charges.
Charges of the same sign: both positive or both negative.
Charges of opposite sign: one positive and one negative.
Insulating rods used in experiments; polythene gains electrons from a cloth (negative), acetate loses electrons to a cloth (positive).

mistakes.w: Positive charges move from the cloth to the acetate rod.
mistakes.r: Electrons move from the acetate rod to the cloth, so the rod is left positive.

mistakes.w: Rubbing creates charge.
mistakes.r: Rubbing transfers electrons; the total charge stays the same.

mistakes.w: The rod gains protons and becomes positive.
mistakes.r: Protons cannot move; the rod loses electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.

mistakes.w: Like charges attract.
mistakes.r: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

mistakes.w: The cloth stays neutral after rubbing.
mistakes.r: The cloth gets a charge equal in size and opposite in sign to the rod.

mistakes.w: Metal rods held in the hand are easy to charge by rubbing.
mistakes.r: Insulators are charged by friction because electrons cannot move through them; charge on a conductor flows away.

mistakes.w: The rod becomes negative because it gains negative energy.
mistakes.r: The rod becomes negative because it gains electrons.

mistakes.w: The force only acts when the rods touch.
mistakes.r: The electrostatic force is a non-contact force; it acts at a distance and is bigger when closer.

exam.q: State the name of the particle transferred when an insulator is charged by friction.
model: Electron
exam.tip: Never proton or positive charge.

exam.q: State what happens when two negatively charged objects are brought close together.
model: They repel / push apart
exam.tip: Like charges repel.

exam.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how it becomes negatively charged.
model: Electrons are transferred from the cloth to the rod (by friction)
The rod has more electrons than protons / gains electrons, so it is negative
exam.tip: Say where the electrons come from.

exam.q: State the charge on the cloth used in the question above and explain why.
model: Positive
The cloth has lost electrons, so it has more protons than electrons / an equal and opposite charge to the rod
exam.tip: Mention 'equal' for full credit in explain questions.

exam.q: An acetate rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. Describe the movement of charge.
model: Electrons move from the acetate rod
to the cloth
exam.tip: Direction is opposite to polythene.

exam.q: Explain why the rod and the cloth attract each other after rubbing.
model: They have opposite / unlike charges
Unlike charges attract
exam.tip: Two clear statements.

exam.q: Explain why an insulator, rather than a metal held in the hand, is used to demonstrate charging by friction.
model: In an insulator electrons cannot move, so the charge stays on the surface
In a metal electrons are free to move, so the charge would flow away (through the hand)
exam.tip: Compare both materials.

exam.q: A charged polythene rod hangs freely. A charged acetate rod is brought near one end. Describe and explain what happens.
model: The hanging rod turns towards the acetate rod / is attracted
Polythene is negative and acetate is positive
Unlike charges attract
exam.tip: Observation, charges, rule.

exam.q: A student rubs a balloon on her hair. The balloon becomes negatively charged. Explain why her hairs then stand on end and spread apart.
model: Electrons are transferred from the hair to the balloon
So each hair loses electrons and becomes positively charged
Like charges repel, so the hairs push away from each other
exam.tip: Each hair has the same type of charge.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a charged polythene rod and a charged acetate rod to show that like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
model: Rub both rods with a cloth to charge them (polythene negative, acetate positive)
Hang one charged rod from a thread so it can turn freely
Bring a second rod of the same material near one end: it turns away, showing like charges repel
Bring a rod of the other material near: it turns towards it, showing unlike charges attract
exam.tip: Include how to charge, how to suspend, both observations.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how rubbing a polythene rod and a cloth together causes both to become charged, and describe the forces between charged objects.
model: Atoms contain protons (positive) in the nucleus and electrons (negative); both objects are initially neutral with equal numbers
Friction transfers electrons from the cloth to the polythene; protons do not move
The polythene gains electrons so becomes negatively charged
The cloth loses electrons so is left with an equal positive charge (charge is conserved)
The charge stays in place because both are insulators
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract; this is a non-contact force that increases as the objects get closer, so the rod and cloth attract
exam.tip: Level 3 answers link particles, transfer, resulting charges and forces in a logical order.

worked.q: Model answer: a Perspex ruler rubbed with a cloth repels a positively charged acetate rod. Deduce the charge on the ruler and on the cloth, and explain how they got these charges.
steps: The ruler repels a positive rod; like charges repel, so the ruler is positive
The ruler became positive by losing electrons
Those electrons were transferred to the cloth by friction
So the cloth gained electrons and is negative, with charge equal in size to the ruler's
worked.ans: Ruler positive (lost electrons), cloth negative (gained the same number of electrons).

worked.q: Applied example: before rubbing, a rod has 1000 protons and 1000 electrons in its surface atoms, and so does a cloth. During rubbing, 12 electrons move from the cloth to the rod. Find the overall charge on each in units of electron charge.
steps: Rod: 1000 protons and 1000 + 12 = 1012 electrons
Rod charge = 1000 - 1012 = -12 units, so negative
Cloth: 1000 protons and 1000 - 12 = 988 electrons
Cloth charge = 1000 - 988 = +12 units, so positive
Total = -12 + 12 = 0, so charge is conserved
worked.ans: Rod -12 units, cloth +12 units: equal and opposite.

worked.q: Applied example: two balloons are both rubbed on a wool jumper and hung side by side on threads. Predict and explain what happens.
steps: Rubbing transfers electrons from the wool to each balloon
Both balloons gain electrons and become negatively charged
Like charges repel, so each balloon experiences a force away from the other
The threads swing apart; the closer they hang, the bigger the force
worked.ans: The balloons push apart because they both carry negative charge and like charges repel.

phy_edx.10.1.summary: Everyday static effects all come down to one idea: only **electrons** move. When electrons build up on an insulator or are removed from it, the object becomes charged, and that charge can attract neutral objects by **induction**, give you a shock, or discharge as lightning. **Earthing** removes excess charge safely by giving electrons a conducting path to or from the Earth until the object is neutral.

core.h: The one rule: only electrons move
core.p: Every static effect at GCSE is explained by the **movement of electrons**. Protons are locked in the nucleus and cannot move between objects, so positive charge never travels.
bullets: An object becomes **negatively charged** when it **gains electrons**.
An object becomes **positively charged** when it **loses electrons**.
A neutral object has equal numbers of protons and electrons; it still contains charges, they are just balanced.
Like charges **repel**; unlike charges **attract**.
Charge builds up on **insulators** because electrons cannot flow through them to spread out or escape.

callouts.p: Writing that positive charges or protons move to or from an object loses the mark every time. Always describe positive charge as a shortage of electrons.

core.h: Attraction by induction: a charged balloon on a wall
core.p: Rub a balloon on your hair or a jumper and it gains electrons, becoming negatively charged. Hold it near a wall and it sticks, even though the wall is **neutral**. This is **attraction by induction**.
bullets: The negative balloon **repels electrons** in the surface of the wall slightly away from the balloon.
This leaves the wall surface nearest the balloon with a **positive** charge (a shortage of electrons) and the region a little further away slightly negative.
The positive surface is **closer** to the balloon than the negative region.
Electrostatic force gets **stronger the closer** the charges are, so the attraction to the near positive charge is bigger than the repulsion from the further negative charge.
Overall there is a **net attractive force** and the balloon sticks.
The wall does not become charged overall: it has only had its charges **separated**, not gained or lost any.

callouts.p: A charged object can attract an uncharged object by inducing an opposite charge on the near surface of the uncharged object.

core.h: A charged comb picking up paper
core.p: A plastic comb pulled through dry hair becomes charged by friction (electrons transferred between hair and comb). It can then lift tiny scraps of neutral paper, which works in exactly the same way as the balloon.
bullets: If the comb is negative, it **repels electrons** in the paper to the far side, leaving the near side **positive**.
The near positive side is attracted more strongly than the far negative side is repelled, so there is a net upward attraction.
The paper is **light**, so the small electrostatic force is greater than its **weight** and it jumps up.
If the comb were positively charged, it would **attract electrons** to the near side of the paper: the paper is still attracted (a charged object attracts a neutral one whichever sign it has).
Sometimes the paper touches the comb, some electrons transfer, the paper becomes the **same charge** as the comb and is then **repelled** and falls away.

callouts.p: Attraction of a neutral object happens whether the charged object is positive or negative. Repulsion is the only proof that something is charged.

core.p: You can build up charge on your body by walking on a nylon carpet, sliding off a car seat or taking off a jumper. Friction transfers electrons between your shoes or clothes and the other material.
bullets: Your body becomes charged (gains or loses electrons), and the charge stays because you are insulated from the ground by your shoes or the carpet.
When you touch a **conductor** that is **earthed** such as a metal door handle, tap, radiator or car door, electrons suddenly **flow** between you and the conductor.
If you are negative, electrons flow **from you to earth**; if you are positive, electrons flow **from earth to you**.
This sudden flow of charge is a small **current** through your body, which you feel as a **shock**; you may see a **spark** jump across the small air gap.
Shocks are worse on **dry** days: damp air and moisture on surfaces let charge leak away slowly, so less builds up.

callouts.p: A shock is a sudden flow of electrons (a current) between a charged object and an earthed conductor.

core.p: Lightning is static electricity on a huge scale. Inside a storm cloud, ice crystals and water droplets rub together as they are carried up and down by air currents, transferring electrons by friction.
bullets: Electrons are transferred so the **bottom of the cloud** usually becomes **negatively charged** and the top positive.
The negative cloud base **repels electrons** in the ground below, inducing a **positive charge** on the ground.
The charge keeps building, so the **potential difference** between cloud and ground becomes extremely large.
Eventually the air (normally an insulator) **breaks down** and becomes **ionised** so it conducts.
A huge number of **electrons flow** through the air from the cloud to the ground: this is the lightning bolt.
The current heats the air so fast it expands explosively, producing **thunder**.

callouts.p: Describe lightning as electrons moving from the negative cloud base to the ground (or between clouds), never as positive charge moving up.

core.p: A spark is a visible discharge through air. It happens when the charge on an object is large enough for electrons to jump across an air gap to a nearby conductor or earthed object.
bullets: Large charge build-up means a **large potential difference** between the object and something nearby.
At a high enough potential difference, air molecules are **ionised** and the air conducts for an instant.
Electrons cross the gap, giving off **light**, **heat** and **sound** (a crackle).
Sparks are more likely when the gap is **small** and the charge is **large**.
Sparks can ignite **flammable** gases, vapours or dust, which is why charge build-up can be dangerous.

core.p: Whether charge builds up depends on what the object is made from.
bullets: In **conductors** (metals), electrons are free to move through the material.
In **insulators** (plastic, rubber, glass, dry wool, polythene), electrons cannot move freely, so charge stays where it was put.
A metal object held in your hand does not stay charged: electrons flow through it and through you to earth.
A metal object can be charged if it is **insulated** from earth (for example on a plastic stand).

core.p: **Earthing** means connecting a charged object to the ground with a **conductor**. The Earth is so huge that it can give or accept any number of electrons without its own charge changing noticeably.
bullets: If the object is **negatively charged**, the excess **electrons flow from the object to earth** through the conductor.
If the object is **positively charged**, **electrons flow from earth to the object**, cancelling the positive charge.
Electrons keep flowing until the object is **neutral** (it has the same potential as the earth).
The charge is removed **gradually and safely** through the wire instead of suddenly as a dangerous spark.
An earthing wire, metal strap, conducting tyre or chain all do the same job.

callouts.p: Connecting a charged object to the earth with a conductor so that electrons can flow to or from the earth, removing the excess charge.
For a positive object, do not say positive charge flows to earth. Say electrons flow from the earth to the object.

core.h: Why earthing prevents shocks and sparks
core.p: Charge only becomes dangerous when it can **build up**. Earthing stops the build-up from happening in the first place.
bullets: Electrons flow away **continuously** as soon as charge is produced, so the charge never gets large.
Without a large charge, the **potential difference** stays small, so there is **no spark**.
No sudden discharge through a person means **no shock**.
This is the reason for earthed metal casings, earthing straps for electronics workers and conducting floors in operating theatres.

callouts.p: Earthing lets electrons flow, so charge does not build up, so the potential difference stays low, so there is no spark or shock.

core.p: Students often confuse charging by friction (which changes the total charge) with induction (which only separates charge).
bullets: **Friction**: electrons are **transferred** from one insulator to another; both end up charged with equal and opposite charges.
**Induction**: no electrons enter or leave the neutral object; electrons are just **pushed or pulled** within it.
**Contact**: touching a charged object can let some electrons transfer, so the second object gets the **same** sign of charge.
**Earthing**: electrons flow until the object is neutral.

head: Process
Electrons gained or lost?
Overall charge of object
rows: No, only moved within the object

core.p: Static questions reward a clear chain of cause and effect using the right words.
bullets: Start with **how** the object got charged (friction, electrons transferred, which way).
State the **sign** of the charge and why (gained or lost electrons).
Explain what the charge does to **electrons** in nearby objects (repels or attracts them).
Use **closer** and **stronger** to explain net attraction in induction.
For discharge, name the **conductor**, the **direction of electron flow** and the result (neutral, no spark).

callouts.p: electrons, transferred, friction, insulator, conductor, repel, attract, induced, earth, neutral, spark, potential difference.

analogy.p: Think of electrons as a crowd of people who can move and the positive nuclei as the fixed seats. A charged balloon is like a celebrity the crowd wants to avoid: as it comes near, people shuffle to the far side of the room, leaving empty seats (positive) near the door. Earthing is like opening a huge exit to an endless car park: extra people can leave, or people can come in to fill empty seats, until every seat has exactly one person. Where it breaks down: real electrons are not choosing to move, they are pushed by electrostatic forces, and in an insulator they can only shift a tiny distance within each atom or molecule rather than walking across the whole room.

terms.d: A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; the only charged particle that moves in static electricity.
Electric charge that builds up and stays on the surface of an object, usually an insulator.
Having gained electrons, so there are more electrons than protons.
Having lost electrons, so there are fewer electrons than protons.
Having equal numbers of protons and electrons, so no overall charge.
A material in which electrons are not free to move, so charge stays where it is placed.
A material, such as a metal, in which electrons are free to move.
Separation of charge in a neutral object caused by a nearby charged object, without any charge being transferred.
The charge that appears on part of a neutral object because of a nearby charged object.
A charged object attracting a neutral object because the opposite induced charge is closer than the like induced charge.
The loss of charge from an object as electrons flow to or from it.
A sudden discharge of electrons across an air gap when the potential difference is large enough to ionise the air.
A very large spark in which electrons flow through the air between a charged cloud and the ground or another cloud.
Connecting a charged object to the earth with a conductor so electrons flow to or from earth until the object is neutral.
The ground, which acts as a huge reservoir that can supply or accept electrons without changing its own charge noticeably.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points; a large p.d. between a charged object and earth makes sparking likely.

mistakes.w: The balloon became positive so protons moved onto it.
mistakes.r: The balloon lost electrons; protons never move in static electricity.

mistakes.w: The wall becomes positively charged when the balloon sticks.
mistakes.r: Charge is induced (separated) in the wall; the wall stays neutral overall, with the near surface positive.

mistakes.w: The balloon sticks because opposite charges attract (no further detail).
mistakes.r: The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall away, leaving the nearby surface positive; the closer opposite charge gives a net attraction.

mistakes.w: Earthing a positive object makes positive charge flow to the ground.
mistakes.r: Electrons flow from the earth to the object until it is neutral.

mistakes.w: Earthing stores the charge safely.
mistakes.r: Earthing removes the charge by letting electrons flow to or from earth, so charge cannot build up.

mistakes.w: Lightning happens because the cloud has too much current.
mistakes.r: Charge builds up, the potential difference between cloud and ground becomes very large, the air ionises and electrons flow through it.

mistakes.w: You get a shock because the door handle is charged.
mistakes.r: You are charged; when you touch the earthed metal, electrons flow suddenly between you and earth.

mistakes.w: Metal rods can easily be charged by rubbing while held in the hand.
mistakes.r: Electrons flow through the metal and your body to earth, so the rod does not stay charged unless it is insulated.

mistakes.w: Paper is attracted to the comb because the paper is charged.
mistakes.r: The paper is neutral; the comb induces charge on it, with the opposite charge on the near side.

exam.q: State the name of the particle that moves when an object becomes charged by friction.
model: Electron
exam.tip: Never write proton or positive charge.

exam.q: A balloon is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain why.
model: Electrons are transferred (by friction)
from the cloth to the balloon / the balloon gains electrons
exam.tip: Say which way the electrons went.

exam.q: Explain why a negatively charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.
model: The balloon repels electrons in the wall (surface)
so the surface of the wall nearest the balloon becomes positively charged (induced charge)
opposite charges attract
the positive charge is closer than the negative charge so the attraction is greater than the repulsion
exam.tip: The closer/stronger point is the one most students miss.

exam.q: A charged comb attracts small pieces of paper. Some pieces jump to the comb and then fall off. Explain why they fall off.
model: Electrons are transferred between the comb and paper on contact
the paper gains the same charge as the comb and is repelled
exam.tip: Contact charging gives the same sign of charge.

exam.q: Explain why a person sometimes receives an electric shock when touching a metal door handle after walking across a nylon carpet.
model: Friction between shoes and carpet transfers electrons
the person becomes charged (charge builds up as they are insulated)
the metal handle is a conductor connected to earth
electrons flow suddenly between the person and earth, which is a current felt as a shock
exam.tip: Name the direction of flow if you have stated the sign of charge.

exam.q: Describe how lightning occurs.
model: Ice particles / water droplets rub together in the cloud
electrons are transferred by friction
the base of the cloud becomes negatively charged
this induces a positive charge on the ground below
the potential difference between cloud and ground becomes very large
the air ionises / becomes a conductor
electrons flow from the cloud to the ground (as a spark)
exam.tip: Six marks means a logical sequence from charging to discharge.

exam.q: Explain how earthing removes the charge from a negatively charged metal sphere.
model: The sphere is connected to earth by a conductor (wire)
excess electrons flow from the sphere to earth
until the sphere is neutral
exam.tip: Always finish with neutral.

exam.q: A metal sphere on an insulating stand is positively charged. It is then connected to earth. Describe the movement of charge.
model: Electrons flow from earth to the sphere
until the sphere is neutral / the positive charge is cancelled
exam.tip: Positive object, electrons come in from earth.

exam.q: Explain why static shocks are more common on dry days.
model: Moist air / water on surfaces conducts
so charge leaks away and does not build up; on dry days charge can build up
exam.tip: Link moisture to conduction.

exam.q: Explain why a metal rod held in the hand cannot be charged by rubbing, but a polythene rod can.
model: Metal is a conductor, electrons can move through it
electrons flow through the rod and the person to earth so charge does not build up
polythene is an insulator so electrons cannot move and the charge stays
exam.tip: Compare both materials explicitly.

worked.q: A student rubs an acetate rod with a cloth. The rod becomes positively charged. She then holds the rod near small pieces of neutral foil, which jump up to it. Explain both observations.
steps: Friction between the rod and cloth transfers electrons from the acetate to the cloth.
The rod has lost electrons, so it is positively charged; the cloth gains electrons and is negative.
Near the foil, the positive rod attracts electrons in the foil to the side nearest the rod.
The near side of the foil becomes negative and the far side positive (induced charge).
The opposite charge is closer, so the attractive force is bigger than the repulsive force.
The net upward force is larger than the weight of the light foil, so it jumps up.
worked.ans: Electrons leave the rod for the cloth; the positive rod induces a negative charge on the near side of the foil and the closer opposite charge gives a net attraction greater than the foil's weight.

worked.q: A negatively charged metal dome on an insulating stand is connected to a water pipe by a copper wire. Describe and explain what happens, and why this is safer than letting a person touch the dome.
steps: The water pipe is connected to earth and copper is a conductor.
Excess electrons on the dome are repelled from each other and flow along the wire to earth.
Electrons continue to flow until the dome is neutral.
The charge leaves gradually through the wire, so the potential difference never gets large enough for a spark.
If a person touched the charged dome, the electrons would flow suddenly through their body to earth, giving a shock.
worked.ans: Electrons flow from the dome through the wire to earth until it is neutral, removing the charge safely without a spark or a current through a person.

phy_edx.10.2.summary: Static charge is **useful** when we deliberately charge droplets so that they **repel** each other into a fine, even spray and are **attracted** to an earthed or oppositely charged target, as in **electrostatic paint sprayers** and **insecticide (crop) sprayers**. Static is **dangerous** when friction from flowing fuel builds up charge on aircraft or tankers, because a **spark** could ignite fuel vapour. **Earthing** and bonding give electrons a safe path to earth so charge never builds up.

core.h: The physics you need to apply
core.p: Every use and danger in this point is built from a few ideas from the rest of the topic: charging by friction, forces between charges, induction and earthing.
bullets: Objects are charged by **gaining or losing electrons**; only electrons move.
**Like charges repel**, **unlike charges attract**.
A charged object can attract a **neutral** object by **inducing** an opposite charge on its near side.
Charge builds up on **insulators** or on conductors that are **insulated from earth**.
A large charge gives a large **potential difference**, which can cause a **spark**.
**Earthing** lets electrons flow to or from earth so charge cannot build up.

callouts.p: For any application question: how it is charged, what repulsion does, what attraction does, and why that is an advantage.

core.p: Car bodies, bicycles and metal furniture are often painted with an **electrostatic spray gun**. The nozzle gives the paint droplets a charge as they leave it (for example by friction, or by a high-voltage nozzle).
bullets: All the paint droplets get the **same charge** (say positive).
Like charges **repel**, so the droplets **spread out** into a **fine, even** spray and do not clump together.
The object being painted is **earthed** or given the **opposite charge**.
The charged droplets are **attracted** to the object, so they move towards it and stick.
Droplets are attracted even to surfaces **facing away** from the gun, so paint wraps round onto the back and into corners (hard to reach areas).
Less paint **misses** the target, so **less is wasted** and there is less overspray in the air.
As paint builds up on one spot it becomes charged and repels more droplets, which move to bare areas, giving an **even coat**.

callouts.p: If the car were not earthed, it would gain the same charge as the paint, then repel the droplets. Earthing lets electrons flow so the car stays attractive to the paint (and becomes oppositely charged by induction).

Physics reason

core.p: Farmers spray crops with insecticide from nozzles on a tractor boom or aircraft. In an **electrostatic crop sprayer** the nozzles give the droplets a charge.
bullets: All droplets have the **same charge**, so they **repel** and spread into a **fine, even** cloud covering a large area.
The droplets induce an **opposite charge** on the plants, which are in contact with the earth, so the droplets are **attracted** to the plants.
Droplets are pulled round to coat the **undersides of leaves** and stems, where insects often live.
Less insecticide **drifts** away in the wind or falls on the soil, so **less is wasted** and there is **less pollution** of the environment.
The farmer can use **less chemical**, which saves money.

callouts.p: The crop sprayer is the paint sprayer applied to plants: repulsion spreads, attraction targets. Use the word induced for the plant's charge.

bullets: **Dust precipitators** in chimneys: smoke particles are charged and then attracted to oppositely charged plates, removing them from waste gases.
**Photocopiers and laser printers**: a charged drum attracts toner powder to the areas that will be printed.
**Defibrillators** use stored charge to deliver a controlled current to restart the heart.
In each case, describe the charging, the attraction or repulsion and why it helps.

core.h: Danger: how fuel flow causes charge
core.p: When fuel flows quickly through a pipe or hose, there is **friction** between the fuel and the inside of the pipe.
bullets: Friction **transfers electrons** between the fuel and the pipe.
The fuel and the pipe, nozzle or vehicle become **charged** with opposite charges.
If the vehicle or tank is **insulated** from the ground (for example by **rubber tyres**), the charge cannot escape and **builds up**.
The bigger the charge, the bigger the **potential difference** between the vehicle and earth (or the hose and the tank).
Eventually a **spark** can jump across a small gap.
Fuel gives off **flammable vapour**; a spark can **ignite** it, causing a **fire or explosion**.

callouts.p: Friction, electrons transferred, charge builds up, large potential difference, spark, ignites fuel vapour, explosion.

core.p: Aircraft take on huge volumes of fuel quickly, so a lot of charge can be produced. The aircraft also gains charge by friction with the **air** while flying.
bullets: Before fuelling, a **bonding (earthing) wire** connects the aircraft and the fuel tanker, and both are connected to **earth**.
This keeps the aircraft, tanker and nozzle at the **same potential**, so there is **no potential difference** for a spark to jump across.
Any charge produced flows as **electrons** through the wire **to or from earth** instead of building up.
Fuel tankers and hoses may also have **conducting** (metal) parts so charge can flow away.
Aircraft tyres are made to be slightly **conducting** so charge can leak to the ground on landing.

callouts.p: Mark schemes want both objects (aircraft and tanker) connected together and to earth. Saying only that the plane is earthed is weaker.

core.p: Road tankers delivering fuel to a filling station, and ships loading fuel, face the same danger.
bullets: The tanker sits on **insulating rubber tyres**, so charge from flowing fuel could build up on it.
The tanker is **earthed** with a cable or strap before unloading starts.
Fuel nozzles at petrol pumps are made of metal and connected to earth.
Drivers are told not to get back into the car during fuelling, because sliding over the seat can charge them and a spark could form when they touch the nozzle again.

core.p: Static build-up is a risk wherever there are flammable materials or sensitive electronics.
bullets: **Flour mills, grain silos and coal mines**: fine dust can explode if ignited by a spark.
**Operating theatres**: some anaesthetic gases are flammable, so floors and equipment are conducting and earthed.
**Electronics**: a static discharge can damage microchips, so workers wear **earthing wrist straps**.
**Lightning** strikes on tall buildings are reduced in harm by lightning conductors that carry charge safely to earth.

core.p: Earthing gives a **conducting path** between the object and the ground. The Earth can accept or supply any number of electrons.
bullets: If the object is negative, **electrons flow from the object to earth**.
If the object is positive, **electrons flow from earth to the object**.

core.p: Six-mark questions on uses or dangers are marked on a logical sequence of physics.
bullets: For a **use**: say how the droplets are charged, that they all have the same charge and so repel, that the target is earthed or oppositely charged and so attracts them, then give the advantages.

For a **danger**: say where the friction is, that electrons are transferred, that charge builds up because the object is insulated, that a spark could occur and ignite fuel vapour, then explain how earthing prevents it.
Always use the words **electrons**, **repel**, **attract**, **earthed** and **spark**.

callouts.p: Use so, because and which means between each step; examiners reward linked reasoning, not a list.

analogy.t: Party guests who dislike each other
analogy.p: Charged paint droplets are like party guests who all dislike each other: they spread out evenly across the room (repulsion), and they all rush towards the one person they want to talk to, the earthed car (attraction). Refuelling without earthing is like a crowd squeezing into a room with the doors locked: pressure builds until someone breaks through violently (the spark). Earthing is opening a fire exit so people can leave steadily. Where it breaks down: droplets do not choose where to go, they are pushed by electrostatic forces, and the spark is a sudden flow of electrons rather than objects moving.

exam.tip: Same charge, repel.

so it attracts the paint droplets

less paint wasted / paint reaches hidden surfaces or back of object

so they repel and form a fine spray

worked.q: A car factory switches from an ordinary paint spray to an electrostatic spray. Write a model answer explaining why this saves money.
steps: The spray nozzle gives all the paint droplets the same (positive) charge.
Like charges repel, so the droplets spread out into a fine, even spray.
The car body is earthed, so it becomes negatively charged by induction and attracts the droplets.
Droplets travel towards the car and are even pulled round to its back and inside corners.
Far less paint misses the car, so less paint is wasted and less needs to be bought.
The coat is even, so fewer cars need to be repainted.
worked.ans: Charged droplets repel to form a fine even spray and are attracted to the earthed car, so less paint is wasted and the coat is even, reducing cost.

worked.q: An aircraft is being refuelled. The engineer forgets to connect the earthing cable. Describe and explain what could happen, and how the cable would have prevented it.
steps: Fuel flowing quickly through the hose rubs against the inside of the hose: friction.
Electrons are transferred between the fuel and the hose, so the aircraft and hose become charged.
The aircraft is insulated from the ground by its tyres, so the charge builds up.
The potential difference between the nozzle and the aircraft (or the ground) becomes large.
A spark jumps across the gap and could ignite the fuel vapour, causing a fire or explosion.
With the earthing cable connected, electrons would flow through the conductor to or from earth as soon as charge was produced, so no charge builds up and no spark forms.
worked.ans: Without earthing, friction builds up charge until a spark ignites fuel vapour; the earthing cable lets electrons flow to earth so charge never builds up.

phy_edx.10.3.summary: Every charged object creates an **electric field** around itself: a region in which another charge feels a **force**. Field lines show the **direction of the force on a small positive charge**, so they point **away from positive** and **towards negative** charges, are **radial** around a point charge and **uniform** (parallel and equally spaced) between charged parallel plates. The closer together the lines, the **stronger** the field, and the field idea explains attraction, repulsion, induction and sparking in static electricity.

core.p: A charged object does not need to touch another to push or pull it. It is surrounded by an **electric field**, and any other charge placed in that field experiences a **non-contact force**.
bullets: A **charged object creates an electric field around itself**.
The electric field is the region where a **charge experiences a force**.
The force can be **attractive** (unlike charges) or **repulsive** (like charges).
The field is strongest **close** to the charged object and gets **weaker with distance**.
A larger charge produces a **stronger** field.

callouts.p: A region around a charged object in which another charge experiences a force.
A charged object creates an electric field around itself.

core.p: We draw electric fields using **field lines** (lines of force). They are a model: they show the direction and strength of the field at each point.
bullets: The **direction** of a field line is the direction of the **force on a small positive charge** placed there.
Lines always start on **positive** charges and end on **negative** charges.
Arrows on the lines point **away from positive** and **towards negative**.
Field lines **never cross**, because a charge at a point can only feel a force in one direction.
Field lines meet the surface of a conductor **at right angles**.
The **closer together** (more concentrated) the lines, the **stronger** the field.

callouts.p: Arrows show the force on a POSITIVE test charge. An electron in the same field feels a force in the opposite direction to the arrows.

core.h: Field around an isolated point charge
core.p: A small charged sphere behaves like a **point charge**. Its field is **radial**: the lines are straight and spread out from the centre like spokes of a wheel.
bullets: **Positive point charge**: radial lines pointing **outwards**, away from the charge.
**Negative point charge**: radial lines pointing **inwards**, towards the charge.
The lines get **further apart** as you move away, showing the field gets **weaker** with distance.
The pattern is the same in every direction (it is really three-dimensional, like a hedgehog).
Draw at least 8 evenly spaced lines with arrows, starting at the surface of the sphere.

callouts.p: Examiners give marks for: lines radial (straight from the centre), evenly spaced, correct arrow direction, and lines touching the charge. Use a ruler.

core.p: When two flat metal plates are placed parallel and connected to a power supply, one becomes positively charged and the other negatively charged. The field between them is **uniform**.
bullets: Field lines are **straight**, **parallel** and **equally spaced** between the plates.
They point from the **positive plate to the negative plate**.
Lines meet the plates **at right angles**.
Because the spacing is the same everywhere, the field has the **same strength** and **direction** at every point between the plates (apart from near the edges).
At the **edges** the lines **curve outwards** and spread out, so the field there is weaker and not uniform.
A **larger potential difference** across the plates or a **smaller gap** gives a stronger field (more concentrated lines).

callouts.p: A field with the same strength and direction at every point, shown by parallel, equally spaced field lines.

core.h: Field strength and the concentration of lines
core.p: The spec asks you to **relate the strength of the field to the concentration of lines**. The density of lines tells you how strong the force on a charge would be.
bullets: Where lines are **close together**, the field is **strong**, so a charge there feels a **large force**.
Where lines are **far apart**, the field is **weak**, so the force is **small**.
Around a point charge, the lines get further apart with distance, so the field **decreases with distance**.
Between parallel plates, the line spacing is constant, so the field is **constant** (uniform).
Sharp points on a charged conductor have very concentrated lines, so the field there is very strong.

callouts.p: The closer together the field lines, the stronger the electric field.

core.h: Forces on charges in a field
core.p: Placing a charge in a field shows how the field produces a force.
bullets: A **positive** charge feels a force **in the direction of the field lines**.
A **negative** charge (such as an electron) feels a force **opposite to the field lines**.
Between parallel plates, a positive charge is pushed towards the negative plate and an electron is pushed towards the positive plate.
The force is the **same** everywhere between the plates because the field is uniform.
A stronger field gives a bigger force on the same charge.

core.h: How the field explains attraction and repulsion
core.p: The electric field is the **link** between two charged objects: each one sits in the field of the other.
bullets: Two like charges each experience a force **away** from the other because each is in the other's field.
Two unlike charges each experience a force **towards** the other.
The forces are **non-contact**: they act across empty space or air.
Because the field is weaker further away, the forces get **smaller as the distance increases**.

core.p: A neutral object brought near a charged object is inside its electric field.
bullets: The field exerts forces on the **electrons** in the neutral object.
Near a negative object, the field pushes electrons **away**, leaving the near side positive.
Near a positive object, the field pulls electrons **towards** the near side, making it negative.
The field is **stronger** closer to the charged object, so the force on the near (opposite) charge is bigger than on the far (like) charge.
This gives a **net attractive** force, which is why a charged balloon sticks to a wall.

callouts.t: Use the field in your answer
callouts.p: For 11.10 questions, mention the field explicitly: the charged object produces a field, the field exerts a force on electrons, the field is stronger nearer the object.

core.p: Sparks happen where the electric field becomes very strong.
bullets: As charge builds up on an object, its electric field gets **stronger**.
The field is strongest between the charged object and a nearby **earthed** conductor, where the lines are **most concentrated**.
When the field is strong enough, it pulls electrons off air molecules: the air becomes **ionised** and conducts.
Electrons then flow across the gap as a **spark** (or as **lightning** on a large scale).
Sparks are more likely across **small gaps** and near **sharp points**, where the field is strongest.

callouts.p: Charge builds up, field becomes very strong, air is ionised, electrons flow through air, spark.

core.p: Learn to recognise and draw each pattern quickly.

core.h: Electric fields and other field types
core.p: Electric fields have similarities with gravitational and magnetic fields, which helps you remember them.
bullets: All three are **non-contact** forces acting in a region called a field.
Magnetic field lines go from north to south; electric field lines go from **positive to negative**.
Gravitational fields only attract; electric fields can **attract or repel**.
In every case, **closer lines** mean a **stronger** field.

core.p: Field questions are often drawing or describing questions.
bullets: Draw lines with a **ruler**, starting and ending on the charged surfaces.
Always add **arrows**; missing arrows is the most common lost mark.
For parallel plates, keep lines **equally spaced** and show curved edge lines if asked for detail.
When asked to explain a static effect using fields, say the object **produces a field**, the field **exerts a force** on charges (electrons), and the field is **stronger closer** to the object.
Do not let field lines cross or start in empty space.

callouts.t: Lines do not touch each other
callouts.p: Two field lines crossing would mean two directions of force at one point, which is impossible.

analogy.t: A garden sprinkler and water pressure
analogy.p: Think of a positive charge as a sprinkler sending water outwards in every direction: the streams (field lines) point away from it and are tightly packed close by, so a nearby leaf gets hit hard (strong field), while far away the streams spread out and a leaf feels only a light spray (weak field). A negative charge is like a drain that everything flows into. Parallel plates are like a wide shower head above a floor drain: evenly spaced straight streams, the same force everywhere. Where it breaks down: nothing actually flows along electric field lines; they are a drawing that shows the direction of the force on a positive charge, and an electron is pushed the opposite way.

terms.d: A region around a charged object in which another charge experiences a force.
A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive charge placed in an electric field.
A charged object so small that its charge can be treated as being at one point, such as a small charged sphere.
A field whose lines spread out straight from a central point, as around a point charge.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
Two flat conducting plates facing each other with opposite charges, producing a uniform field between them.
How large the force on a charge is at a point in the field; shown by how concentrated the field lines are.
How close together the field lines are; more concentrated means a stronger field.
The curving and spreading of field lines at the ends of parallel plates, where the field is not uniform.
A small positive charge used to find the direction of the force in a field.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as the electrostatic force.
The force between charged objects: like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Air in which molecules have lost electrons, so it can conduct and allow a spark.
A sudden discharge of electrons through air caused by a very strong electric field.
Separation of charge in a neutral object by the electric field of a nearby charged object.

mistakes.w: Field lines point from negative to positive.
mistakes.r: Field lines point from positive to negative (the direction of the force on a positive charge).

mistakes.w: Field lines around a negative charge point outwards.
mistakes.r: They point radially inwards, towards the negative charge.

mistakes.w: Field lines show the direction electrons move.
mistakes.r: They show the direction of force on a positive charge; electrons are pushed the opposite way.

mistakes.w: The field between parallel plates is strongest in the middle.
mistakes.r: The field is uniform: the same strength everywhere between the plates (except at the edges).

mistakes.w: Lines further apart mean a stronger field.
mistakes.r: Lines closer together (more concentrated) mean a stronger field.

mistakes.w: Drawing lines between plates that are not equally spaced or that curve in the middle.
mistakes.r: Straight, parallel, equally spaced lines at right angles to the plates.

mistakes.w: Field lines can cross where two fields meet.
mistakes.r: Field lines never cross; the force at each point has only one direction.

mistakes.w: An electric field only exists around moving charges.
mistakes.r: Any charged object, including a stationary one, creates an electric field around itself.

exam.q: State what is meant by an electric field.
model: A region in which a charge experiences a force
exam.tip: Region plus force on a charge.

exam.q: Draw the electric field around an isolated positively charged sphere.
model: Radial lines starting at the surface of the sphere, evenly spaced
arrows pointing outwards
exam.tip: Use a ruler and at least eight lines.

exam.q: Describe how the electric field around a negative point charge differs from that around a positive point charge.
model: The lines point inwards (towards the charge) instead of outwards
exam.tip: Shape is the same; only direction changes.

exam.q: Draw the electric field between two oppositely charged parallel plates.
model: Straight parallel lines between the plates
equally spaced and at right angles to the plates
arrows from positive plate to negative plate
exam.tip: Arrows are usually one full mark.

exam.q: Describe the electric field between two parallel plates.
model: Uniform / same strength and direction everywhere
lines point from the positive plate to the negative plate
exam.tip: Use the word uniform.

exam.q: Explain how the field lines show where the field around a point charge is strongest.
model: The lines are closest together / most concentrated near the charge
so the field is strongest near the charge and weaker further away
exam.tip: Link concentration to strength.

exam.q: An electron is placed between two charged parallel plates. State the direction of the force on it and explain your answer.
model: Towards the positive plate / opposite to the field lines
because the electron is negative and field lines show the force on a positive charge
exam.tip: Electrons go against the arrows.

exam.q: Explain, using the idea of an electric field, why a negatively charged balloon is attracted to a neutral wall.
model: The balloon produces an electric field around it
the field exerts a force on electrons in the wall, pushing them away from the surface
the near surface becomes positive
the field is stronger closer to the balloon so the attraction is greater than the repulsion
exam.tip: Bring the field into every step.

exam.q: Explain how the concept of an electric field explains why a spark can jump from a charged dome to an earthed sphere.
model: The charged dome creates an electric field
as charge builds up the field becomes stronger
the field is strongest in the gap between the dome and the earthed sphere / lines most concentrated
a strong field ionises the air
ionised air conducts so electrons flow across the gap
this sudden flow of electrons is the spark
exam.tip: A logical sequence from field to ionisation to electron flow.

exam.q: Explain why field lines never cross.
model: The field line direction is the direction of the force on a charge
a charge at one point can only feel a force in one direction
exam.tip: Two directions at one point is impossible.

worked.q: Two parallel metal plates are connected to a high voltage supply. The top plate is positive. A small positively charged oil drop and a free electron are between the plates. Describe the field and the forces on each particle.
steps: The field is uniform between the plates: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.
The lines point from the top (positive) plate down to the bottom (negative) plate.
The positive oil drop feels a force in the direction of the field: downwards, towards the negative plate.
The electron is negative, so it feels a force opposite to the field: upwards, towards the positive plate.
Because the field is uniform, each force has the same size wherever the particle is between the plates.
worked.ans: Uniform field downwards from positive to negative plate; the oil drop is pushed down, the electron is pushed up, each with a constant force.

worked.q: A student draws the field around a small positively charged sphere and says the field is the same strength at all points. Write a model answer correcting this.
steps: The field around a point charge is radial: lines spread outwards from the sphere.
Near the sphere, the lines are close together (concentrated), so the field is strong.
Further away, the lines are spread out, so the field is weaker.
So a charge placed close to the sphere feels a larger force than the same charge placed further away.
Only between parallel plates is the field uniform (same strength everywhere).
worked.ans: The field is not the same everywhere: it is strongest near the sphere, where lines are concentrated, and gets weaker with distance as the lines spread out.
